opening.spoken: This record covers the claimed solution of The Riemann Hypothesis: what has been claimed, what it rests on, and what would have to be checked by whom.

short_version.spoken: On 20 November 2026 Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a four-page note on his personal site saying that he believes he has, working with Claude, found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, that the method also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, and that the argument has been formalized in Lean 4 without extra assumptions. He released no paper, only the Lean code. Nervous Machine fetched the archive the same day and pinned it by hash. It holds 175,187 Lean files, about 17.4 million lines, built against a pinned Mathlib. Its entry file states Mathlib's own definition RiemannHypothesis as its main result. Andrew Sutherland at MIT reports an independent compile, axiom audit and kernel replays, and on 21 November the Lean and Mathlib communities issued a joint statement saying they certify the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. Nervous Machine's own pre-registered build, halted once by a full disk and resumed, compiled every module, found no sorry or axiom in the source, confirmed the three standard axioms for each of the five theorems, and confirmed that the main statement is Mathlib's; that finding is accepted. Nothing is certified, because two independent builds match byte for byte only on the files that carry no source path. No independent mathematician has reported reading the argument, and nobody has signed or refused what the statements mean.

what_happened.spoken: The claim was pinned from the public record by commit or hash. A reading guide for the five statements was written. The first pre-registered build ran three hours and stopped on a full disk, our fault; the resumed build finished the next day: every module compiles, the source has no sorry or axiom, the five theorems rest on the standard axioms, and the main statement is Mathlib's. Our output matches Andrew Sutherland's byte for byte on 76,968 files including the entry file, and differs on 98,219 only by the source path the compiler writes into warned modules. The Lean and Mathlib communities issued a joint statement the same day. Nobody has yet signed or refused the reading guide.

rely_on.spoken: that the released Lean code compiles against Mathlib and its five theorems follow from Lean's three standard axioms, with the main statement being Mathlib's RiemannHypothesis

do_not_rely_on.spoken: the claim as a settled theorem of mathematics: no independent mathematician has read the argument (EG3), nobody has signed or refused what the formal statements mean (EG2, EG4), and the record's certification rule has not been met (EG5)

certainty_statement.spoken: One finding is accepted: the archive builds, its source has no escape hatch, its five theorems rest on the three standard axioms, and its main statement is Mathlib's Riemann Hypothesis. Nothing is certified. Whether the statements mean what the problem asks, and whether anyone understands the argument, is open.

cycles.spoken: Our first build of the archive ran for three hours and nineteen minutes and stopped when the machine's disk filled. The disk was our mistake: the build tool writes a large bookkeeping file for every module, and we had not planned for it. Thirty-two thousand of the hundred and seventy-five thousand modules compiled before the halt, with no error other than the full disk. We compared those with the hashes Andrew Sutherland published: about half agree byte for byte. The other half differ because the compiler writes the absolute path of each source file into the output of any module that produced a warning, so two builds in different directories cannot match on those modules. The build is resumed as cycle 2, written down first.

cycles.spoken: What the public record added on 21 November. The Lean and Mathlib communities published a joint statement, which the page says is endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, saying they certify both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis: dozens of independent compilations reproducing the same exported proof, two tools confirming the proved theorem is Mathlib's statement, and several checkers accepting the export. Its conclusion does not follow from them as stated. cycles.spoken: On 24 November Nervous Machine put the proof beside three thousand Mathlib proofs, measured the same way. A large Mathlib proof is a fan: its mass meets at the theorem itself, four fifths of it, and the spine is down to a tenth by the third step. The archive is a chain: it holds everything for three steps and two thirds at the fifth, and its largest joint gathers a quarter. It has twice the hinges and they are half the length, four lines against ten, shorter than in any of the hundred Mathlib proofs; thirty-two of them carry a rewrite mark where Mathlib's carry none, and its rate of rewrite marks is thirty-eight times Mathlib's. One subject directory holds forty-four percent of its lines against a Mathlib sixteen. What it shares with Mathlib is substrate: in both, the largest directory is reached from everywhere and dominated by nothing in itself, which the operating agent had taken for a peculiarity and registered as one; that prediction missed. Five of seven held. The ten largest Mathlib proofs in the sample are all about L-functions, number fields and modular forms, the ground the archive stands on. Nothing changed standing.

cycles.spoken: On 24 November Nervous Machine tried the general-relativity test on the proof: do the wings that meet at a joint come from different parts of the library, and had those parts been joined before? At the resolution of Mathlib's directory tree the test has nothing to say. The proof reaches twenty-five of twenty-six directories and every wing of every large joint reaches nearly all of them, so no joint brings together anything its wings did not already share; Mathlib's own large proofs behave the same way, four in a hundred showing any crossing at all. Two things survive: the archive's wings are more alike than Mathlib's, which fits a chain of stages rather than a fan of inputs, and the archive uses almost all of Mathlib where no sampled Mathlib proof uses more than twenty of its directories. The finer instrument is a new registration. Five of six predictions held, one of them hollow and marked so. Nothing changed standing.

The test came unstuck and then failed the other way: sixteen of the proof's twenty joints now bring together directories their wings do not share, and so do a quarter of Mathlib's own large joints, but every such pair, on both sides, is one that no Mathlib theorem has ever depended on together, so the rarity score is zero for everyone and tells nothing apart. No choice of directory depth measures whether the ideas joined had met before; that needs the published theorems each wing rests on, which is a reading with a bibliography. What both depths agree on is that the proof's wings draw on nearly the same library where Mathlib's do not, the mark of stages on one route rather than inputs to a fan. cycles.spoken: A short check, filed because its answer closes a door. The release tarball of the proof carries no dates: every file is stamped with the Unix epoch, owned by nobody, and listed in alphabetical order. That is how a reproducible build is packaged, and it is good practice, but it also means that nothing in the release says what was written first and what last. The dependency tree can be measured; its history cannot. The one chronology that exists is the record of attempts, which has not been published.

public_reactions.what: Lists four "stupid things I did". The figure of 250,000+ pages was a joke; he finds big numbers funny and did not correct it in the days after the announcement. The Lean is "full of garbage obviously, but compiles"; criticism of it is reasonable; he should have cleaned it up and found that hard "for various strange reasons". He was "yoloing a lot in there", bets most of it is unnecessary, and expects it to simplify massively. His stated point: arguments like these are raw inputs for interpolating definitions; there is no H^1 object over number fields yet; Riemann should be easy, and any real difficulty indicates the current setup is wrong.
public_reactions.note: The claimant's own account of the artifact. It changes nothing about correctness: the main theorem's type and the kernel's acceptance (finding F1) are facts about the archive, not about its author's tidiness, and the Lean and Mathlib communities' statement of 21 November stands. It changes three things about how the rest of this record should be read. First, the 250,000-page document that several readings, this record's own notes and the public ask for an attempt record referred to does not exist as described; what record of attempts exists, and in what form, is unknown, and the ask is now for whatever that record is. Second, the archive's size carries no information about effort or method by the author's own statement, which agrees with what the traces measured without knowing it: a third of the archive's constants unused, rewrite marks on 33 of 81 hinges, the chain shape, the author's own expectation that "most is unnecessary". The shape traces measured a deliberately uncleaned artifact and should be read as such; the dominator tree is still the tree of what the kernel uses. cycles.spoken: Three days after the release the claimant posted a list of his own mistakes. The two hundred and fifty thousand pages were a joke that got away from him. He wrote no account he thought readable and put everything into Lean, which he calls full of garbage, though it compiles, and which he expects to shrink a great deal once someone does the work. He says criticism of it is fair. None of that touches the check: the theorem has the right type and the kernel accepts it, and that was never about tidiness. What it changes is how to read the size. The traces of the past two days found a third of the archive unused, rewriting concentrated at the joins, and a shape unlike any proof in Mathlib; the author now says, in effect, that this is what it is. And the document this record and others asked to see does not exist in the form everyone named. Whatever record of attempts does exist, in whatever size, is the ask now. A reaction the same evening called the release a stunt and tied it to the timing of Masullo's draft; that is one person's account of motives, and this record keeps to what the documents say.

background.spoken: Every zero of the Riemann zeta function that is not a negative even integer lies on the line where the real part equals one half. The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis says the same of the zeros of every Dirichlet L-function in the critical strip. Mathlib, the Lean mathematical library, states the Riemann Hypothesis as a definition named RiemannHypothesis: for every complex s with zeta of s equal to zero, s not of the form minus two times a positive integer, and s not equal to one, the real part of s is one half.

background.spoken: The note says the author believes he has found, with Claude, a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, that the method extends to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and that both have been formalized in Lean without assumptions. It describes the argument as a descendant of Stepanov's method over function fields, with chains of theta lifts between definite unitary groups standing in for multiplicity, and gives a twenty-step timeline from 6 October to 16 November 2026 that the author says Claude compiled. The note says the argument is very long, that the author has not mastered all of the mathematics it uses, that parts of his description paraphrase an AI-written summary and may be wrong, and that he chose to release only the Lean code rather than an informal write-up. The archive has no README, licence or build instructions. Its lakefile names eleven build targets and raises the default heartbeat and stack limits. The entry file Main.lean states five results: Mathlib's RiemannHypothesis, and four statements the claimant defines in Statements.lean about zeros and non-vanishing of Dirichlet L-functions.
